label: Afternoon edition
summary: Keanu, Monday brought a market bounce, a busy election week and a Wednesday strike in California. **Stocks rebounded from last week's AI selloff**, with the S&P 500 up 0.41% and the Nasdaq up 1.11%, though CoreWeave and Oracle debt still looks stressed (CNBC, Bloomberg). Amazon jumped about 5% on a Morgan Stanley call, and Tesla reports Wednesday after the close (CNBC). **Trump's Russia sanctions waiver is drawing fire** from a bipartisan group of senators and from Zelensky, while Bessent and Wright defend it (The Hill, Fox News, Washington Examiner). Trump rallied in Kansas, where Sen. Roger Marshall is in a toss-up race, and Zelensky says Trump is pushing Ukraine to yield (CNN, Bloomberg). Federal prosecutors charged 28 green card holders in California as the Justice Department sues the state over voter rolls (CalMatters, Fox News). **State workers strike Wednesday**, the first walkout in the history of SEIU Local 1000, and BART says up to 15 stations could close if the Nov. 3 transit tax fails (CalMatters, KQED, San Francisco Chronicle). Traders put the odds that the Fed holds on Oct. 28 above 80% after September CPI hit 3.7% (CNBC, Fox Business). Anthropic pledged 5% of its shares to a public benefit fund and Musk promised every US child a SpaceX share (CNBC, NBC News). Webb found the farthest known fast radio burst's home galaxy, and **NASA says Orion's heat shield performed as expected** on Artemis II (NASA, Space.com).

alerts.text: SEIU Local 1000's one-day state worker strike is Wednesday, Oct. 21; expect possible delays at the DMV and state benefit offices.
Tesla reports Wednesday after the close, then Alphabet and Microsoft on Oct. 28 and Amazon on Oct. 29; Amazon rose about 5% today.
BART says it could close up to 15 stations if the Nov. 3 regional transit tax fails, and Alameda County voters will see it on the ballot.
The Fed meets Oct. 27-28; traders see a hold as more than 80% likely after 3.7% September inflation.

Chips snap an eight-day losing streak, but CoreWeave and Oracle credit still looks stressed.

stories.title: Republicans and Democrats keep pushing Trump to reverse his Russia sanctions waiver
stories.summary: A dozen senators, Speaker Johnson and Zelensky object to Trump's Graham Act waiver while Bessent and Wright defend it as a path to peace.
story: President Trump signed an order on Friday, Oct. 16, waiving the main penalties in the Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, two days before they were due to take effect. The backlash kept building through the weekend. The Hill reported that Sen. Thom Tillis called the move "beyond irresponsible" and that Sen. Darline Graham, who holds her late brother's seat, said she would keep pressure on Russia. Fox News reported that six Republican senators joined six Democrats in a letter calling the separate diesel deal "a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies."

The waiver sits on top of an Oct. 9 diesel license that allows trade in Russian-origin diesel. CNN reports the order suspends tariffs on Russian imports and on the five biggest buyers of Russian oil and gas, while The Hill describes it mainly as relief on Russian energy sanctions. The administration says it needs room for peace talks. Trump said he is "in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine" (The Hill).

Defenders of the order are mostly inside the administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Meet the Press that "no one has been tougher" on Russia than Trump (Washington Examiner), and Energy Secretary Chris Wright called the diesel waiver "a carrot to try to end a war" and said it is "not an economic lifeline" for Russia (Fox News, The Hill). Rep. Thomas Massie, a frequent Trump critic, praised the waiver (Washington Examiner). Speaker Mike Johnson said he warned the White House of "unintended consequences" (The Hill). Sen. Ted Cruz said he wished Trump had not done it (Fox News).

The test is whether Congress can force a president to use a law it passed over his objections. With diesel prices a midterm issue and Zelensky calling the policy a "historic mistake" (CNN), the pressure to reverse or defend it will continue until Nov. 3.
facts: Trump signed the Graham Act waiver on Friday, Oct. 16, two days before the penalties were due to start.
Six Republican senators, including Tillis, Collins, Murkowski and McConnell, joined six Democrats in urging Trump to scrap the diesel deal (Fox News).
Bessent and Wright defend the order as leverage for peace talks.
Speaker Johnson said he warned the White House about "unintended consequences" (The Hill).
Outlets differ on scope: CNN says tariffs on Russian imports and top oil buyers are suspended; The Hill focuses on energy sanctions.
stories.flag: CNN and The Hill describe the scope of the waiver differently; the exact text of the order was not reviewed.
stories.left: Democrats and the Ukraine-hawk wing of both parties argue that Congress wrote the Graham Act to bind Putin and that Trump waived it before it could bite. They say easing diesel and tariff pressure while Ukraine runs short of air defense rewards Moscow for the war. Sen. Schumer ripped the waiver, and Zelensky says siding with Russia is a historic mistake. The strongest version of the case is that a sanctions law with a presidential escape hatch is only as strong as the president's will.
stories.right: Administration allies argue that a president needs flexibility to close a war, and that a diesel market squeezed by the Iran conflict hurts American drivers and truckers. Bessent says no one has been tougher on Russia, and Wright calls the waiver a carrot that can be pulled back. Rep. Massie, a frequent Trump critic, praised the move. Conservative critics such as Tillis and Cruz answer that the carrot arrives before Putin has given anything.
stories.next: Watch for a Senate vote or letter campaign to rescind the waiver, and for any Putin-Trump meeting; Bloomberg reports Putin proposed one with Xi next month.

stories.title: Federal prosecutors charge 28 in California as the Justice Department fights the state over voter rolls
stories.summary: DOJ sued to block ballots from about 20,000 suspected noncitizens, then charged 28 green card holders; state officials call the numbers unsupported.
story: Federal prosecutors charged 28 people in California on Monday, Oct. 19, in a voter-registration crackdown. CalMatters and KQED report that all 28 are green card holders, not citizens, and that 22 are accused of voting, including in the June primary. The Washington Examiner and Fox News report that agents arrested at least 11 suspects Monday morning. The charges include false statements on naturalization applications and fraudulent voter registration.

The arrests followed a federal lawsuit filed last Thursday in Los Angeles. It asks a judge to bar California from counting mail ballots from about 20,000 voters the government suspects are noncitizens (CNN, CalMatters). The Justice Department gave officials 48 hours to review a thumb drive of names. Los Angeles County officials said they did not open the drive because it did not meet the registrar's security standards (CNN). Trump wrote that election workers who count such ballots "will all go to jail for a long period of time" (The Hill).

California officials say the case is thin. Attorney General Rob Bonta said the 28 defendants amount to 0.0001% of registered voters, and more than 9.4 million Californians voted in the June primary (KQED). The figure the administration cited in July was 190,000, and it has dropped to 20,000 (CNN). Legal experts called the lawsuit a "long shot" (CNN). Fox News reports the Justice Department has not established that the people on its list cast illegal ballots. Secretary of State Shirley Weber's office says the federal government has not shared its evidence or methods.
The dispute lands 15 days before the election, when the National Voter Registration Act limits changes to voter rolls. California officials argue the 90-day pre-election window bars removals.
facts: Prosecutors charged 28 people Monday; 22 are accused of voting, including in the June primary (CalMatters, KQED).
The DOJ lawsuit seeks to block counting ballots from about 20,000 suspected noncitizens.
DOJ gave California 48 hours to review the list; Los Angeles County did not open the thumb drive.
The estimate of suspected noncitizens fell from 190,000 in July to 20,000 (CNN).
Bonta says the defendants equal 0.0001% of registered voters.
stories.flag: The DOJ has not shown that the roughly 20,000 people on its list voted illegally; only the 28 charged are tied to specific allegations.
stories.left: Democrats and election officials argue the administration is manufacturing a crisis to sow doubt about California's results. They point to the shrinking list, a 48-hour deadline, a thumb drive and a lawsuit judges are expected to reject, as the Justice Department has lost every ruling so far in its voter-data suits (CalMatters). Threatening election workers with jail, they say, is intimidation. The 28 cases show the system catches fraud, which is rare.
stories.right: Republicans argue that noncitizen voting, however rare, undermines trust and that a state that will not review a federal list is hiding the problem. They note that 22 defendants allegedly voted and that prosecutors have brought cases in 17 states (Fox News). Conservative writers say verifying citizenship is a basic duty and that the federal government has standing to demand it. Election integrity, in this view, does not depend on how few cases there are.
stories.next: Watch for a ruling on the Los Angeles lawsuit before ballots are counted, and for more arrests; election day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

stories.title: Trump rallies in Kansas as a deep-red Senate seat becomes competitive
stories.summary: Trump campaigned for Sen. Roger Marshall near Wichita, said the polls are fake, and starts a week of travel to Senate battlegrounds.
story: President Trump rallied Monday, Oct. 19, in Park City, outside Wichita, for Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who is in a tight race with Democrat Adam Hamilton (Fox News, The Hill, CNN). Trump told reporters the polls are "fake" while also saying he is tied or slightly ahead in them (CNN). The Hill reports he begins his busiest travel week of the cycle, with stops planned in Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa, Florida, Georgia and Michigan.

Kansas is a state Trump won by more than 16 points in 2024. RealClearPolling's average has Marshall ahead by 0.3 points, and Cook Political Report rates the race a toss-up (CNN, NPR). A New York Times/Siena poll earlier this month showed the two tied, and an Emerson College poll had Hamilton up 2 points (NPR, Washington Examiner). Fox News reports Trump is pushing his immigration agenda in the state as ICE arrests increase.

Axios frames the race as part of a broader risk to decades-old Republican winning streaks. NPR notes that Trump's travel list includes many very red states, not the swing districts he had promised. In one recent poll cited by CNN, 40% approved of Trump's job performance and 53% disapproved. An AP-NORC poll found about 6 in 10 Hispanic voters disapprove of his presidency, with high prices a leading complaint.
The Kansas race shows how wide the Senate map has become, with Republicans spending time in states they usually win.
facts: Trump rallied for Sen. Roger Marshall in Park City, Kansas, on Monday, Oct. 19.
RealClearPolling's average has Marshall ahead by 0.3 points; Cook rates the race a toss-up.
Trump won Kansas by more than 16 points in 2024.
Trump plans stops in at least seven states this week, including NC, SC, Iowa, Florida, Georgia and Michigan.
One recent poll shows Trump at 40% approval and 53% disapproval (CNN).
stories.left: Democrats say a Kansas Senate race this close shows voters are punishing Republicans for high gas and diesel prices, the Iran war and aggressive immigration enforcement. They argue that Trump visiting red states is a defensive move, not a show of strength.  A win would signal a wave that reaches well beyond the swing districts.
stories.right: Republicans argue that Kansas is still a red state and that polls have underestimated Trump voters before. They say the president's rally will turn out base voters, and that immigration enforcement is a winning message there. Conservative writers add that tight polls are a reason to campaign, not proof of a wave.
stories.next: Watch Trump's stops this week and the next round of Kansas polls; the election is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

stories.title: California's largest state worker union holds its first strike on Wednesday
stories.summary: SEIU Local 1000 plans a one-day walkout Oct. 21 over pay, health costs and telework as a state mediator joins the talks.
story: SEIU Local 1000, which represents about 100,000 California state workers, plans a one-day strike on Wednesday, Oct. 21. CalMatters and KQED report that 96.2% of voting members authorized it. Office workers, cooks, custodians, nurses and others are expected to take part. The union's president warned that services could be delayed at the DMV and at the state's unemployment and disability insurance offices (CalMatters).

The union wants higher pay, more affordable health coverage and more flexibility to work from home. Its contract expired June 30. It has never held a statewide walkout in the 44-year history of the groups that became Local 1000 (CalMatters). Newsom wants workers in the office four days a week and vetoed AB 1729, which would have let departments set their own remote-work rules (CalMatters).

In late September, the Public Employment Relations Board sided with the union and found the state "refused to meet and confer in good faith," then appointed a mediator (KQED). The California Department of Human Resources says the state "remains open to negotiation" and is ready for mediation. Local 1000 President Anica Walls said "Administrations change, but our demands won't," a signal that the union will hold out past Newsom's term.
I found no state contingency plan for DMV service on Wednesday, so Fremont residents with appointments that day should check before going.
facts: The one-day strike is set for Wednesday, Oct. 21.
96.2% of voting members authorized it.
Local 1000 represents about 100,000 state workers; the contract expired June 30.
PERB found the state did not bargain in good faith and appointed a mediator.
Newsom vetoed AB 1729 on telework flexibility.
stories.blindspot: Covered mainly by CalMatters and KQED; no right-leaning coverage found.
stories.left: Labor advocates argue that state workers have gone months without a contract while health costs rise and the governor insists on a four-day office mandate. They point to the labor board's finding of bad-faith bargaining as proof the state is stalling. A strike, they say, is the only leverage workers have against an outgoing administration.
stories.right: Fiscal conservatives argue that California faces budget pressure and that raises must be weighed against state budget pressure. They say a strike by public employees punishes residents who need the DMV and benefit offices, and that return-to-office rules protect downtown economies and accountability. The state, they note, has offered mediation and says it is ready to bargain. Taxpayers, in this view, are the party not at the table.
stories.next: Watch whether the state and union agree to mediation dates before Wednesday's walkout.

stories.title: BART and Muni warn of deep cuts if the Nov. 3 regional transit tax fails
stories.summary: The Bay Area measure would raise about $1 billion a year; BART says it could close up to 15 stations without it.
story: Bay Area voters will decide the Regional Transit Measure, also called Connect Bay Area, on Tuesday, Nov. 3. It would add a half-cent sales tax in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties and a one-cent tax in San Francisco, raising about $1 billion a year for 14 years, mostly for operations at BART, AC Transit, Muni and Caltrain (KQED, San Francisco Chronicle). It needs a simple majority.

The agencies say the alternative is service loss. BART has said it could close up to 15 stations, Caltrain says it could close 10, and Muni plans to cut 20 routes (San Francisco Chronicle). SPUR projects the agencies would close their lowest-ridership stations. KQED cites a report finding that Bay Bridge traffic delays would double if the measures fail.

Opponents say the case is overstated. The Contra Costa Taxpayers Association argues that agencies could pause projects like BART Silicon Valley Phase II and high-speed rail, fund operations, and return with a smaller tax in 2028 (KQED). Supporters call that unrealistic because most capital money cannot be used for operations. The SF Chronicle's editorial board endorsed the measure.

The politics are hard. The Chronicle notes that several tax measures failed in the June primary and that suburban voters have been less supportive than San Francisco voters in early polling. The polls I found are earlier ones and showed 55% to 56% support. Fremont is in Alameda County, so its voters will see the measure.
facts: The measure is on the Nov. 3 ballot and needs a simple majority.
It adds a half-cent sales tax in four counties and one cent in San Francisco.
It would raise about $1 billion a year for 14 years.
BART has said it could close up to 15 stations if it fails; Caltrain says 10 stations.
The polls found are earlier ones and showed 55% to 56% support.
stories.flag: No recent poll was found; the 55% to 56% figures are from earlier polling.
stories.blindspot: Coverage found comes from the SF Chronicle and KQED; no right-leaning outlet covered it.
stories.left: Transit advocates argue that cuts would fall hardest on workers who cannot drive and would push more cars onto the Bay Bridge and freeways. They say transit has been underfunded for decades and that a regional sales tax spreads the cost widely. A failed measure would lock in a service-cut spiral that lowers ridership further. Climate and equity goals also depend on a working network.
stories.right: Skeptics argue that agencies should show reforms and cost control before asking for $14 billion in new taxes, especially with voters rejecting tax measures in June. They point to costly capital projects and say operations could be funded by pausing them. Some say a smaller measure in 2028 would be a better deal. In this view, the threat of closures is a negotiating tactic, not a certainty.
stories.next: Watch for new polling and for the agencies to name which stations would close; the vote is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

stories.title: Trump endorses Netanyahu as Iran dares the US to strike again and Qatar plans a defense pact
stories.summary: Trump tied his endorsement to the Iran war nine days before Israel's vote; Iran warns of "unfinished jobs" and oil stays near $98.
story: President Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday, Oct. 18, nine days before the Oct. 27 Knesset election. Axios, CNN and Fox News report he posted a "Complete and Total Endorsement," and Fox reports he linked it to Iran, saying that if Israelis pick someone else, the U.S. would have to finish the job against Iran alone. Most polls show Netanyahu's coalition short of the 61 seats needed to govern (CNN, Axios). His main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, said only Israeli citizens will decide.

The war started in February with U.S. and Israeli strikes. An April ceasefire and a June agreement later collapsed, and Trump has said he will not strike Iran before the midterms (Axios, Fox News). On Monday, Fox News reported that Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, warned the U.S. and Israel against renewed attacks, saying Iran also has "unfinished jobs." Qatar's deputy prime minister said a regional defense partnership with several Middle Eastern countries will be announced in the coming days.

Oil reflects the stalemate. Bloomberg reported that West Texas Intermediate traded around $98 on Monday and that Brent settled at $109.55, near a five-month high, as Iranian threats competed with strong Gulf flows. Live data show WTI at $98.15. Axios reported in September that U.S. officials think Trump could order a return to major combat operations after the midterms.
Analysts disagree on how much Trump's endorsement helps Netanyahu inside Israel (Axios).
facts: Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday, Oct. 18; Israel votes Oct. 27.
Fox reports Trump tied the endorsement to finishing the Iran job.
Brent settled at $109.55 and WTI traded near $98 (Bloomberg).
Qatar says it will announce a regional defense partnership within days.
Araghchi warned the U.S. and Israel they have "unfinished jobs" (Fox News).
stories.left: Critics argue that a U.S. president endorsing a foreign leader while threatening that America will fight Iran alone treats an Israeli election as a lever in the war. They say the war has raised gas and diesel prices at home, killed ceasefire gains and been put on pause only for the midterms. Democrats want Congress to vote on any renewed war. Diplomacy through Qatar and Pakistan, they note, has produced little.
stories.right: Supporters argue that Netanyahu has been the steadiest ally against a regime that attacks shipping and Gulf states, and that a clear signal strengthens deterrence. Conservative hawks such as Marc Thiessen and Mark Levin say a paused war lets Iran recover and that any deal must include verifiable nuclear limits (Washington Examiner). Others on the right worry about the economic cost and about open-ended commitments. Backing allies who fight Iran, in their view, is the core of the policy.
stories.next: Watch the Qatar defense announcement this week and Israel's Oct. 27 vote.

stories.title: Zelensky accuses Trump of pushing Ukraine to yield as the Starshield dispute continues
stories.summary: After Ukraine hit a Russian oil terminal, Trump said Zelensky never wanted peace; Zelensky says Washington is pressing Kyiv to capitulate.
story: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 18 that Trump is pushing Ukraine to capitulate to Russia, escalating a weeklong dispute (Bloomberg). He told NBC's Meet the Press that the U.S. siding with Russia would be a "historic mistake" (CNN). Ukraine had hit a major Russian oil terminal on Sunday in one of its biggest drone attacks this year, defying Trump's demand to stop striking Russian energy sites. Trump responded that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did" (CNN).

Zelensky offered to stop striking Russian refineries in return for more Patriot missiles (CNN). CNN reported earlier that Ukraine has run out of Patriot interceptors. Bloomberg reports Vladimir Putin proposed a meeting with Trump and China's Xi Jinping next month; Ukraine's foreign minister said that would encourage Putin to keep fighting.

A second fight involves Starshield, the military version of Starlink. NPR and Fox News report that Ukraine found its service limited on platforms moving 100 mph or faster. Musk wrote that "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Trump said "it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," and Secretary of State Rubio called the claim "categorically false" (CNN, NPR). Four Republican senators joined Democrats in asking the Pentagon inspector general to investigate (The Hill). Ukraine says access is back; Zelensky says the limits are not fully lifted (NPR).
The dispute arrives as the U.S. waives Russia sanctions, and it narrows the options for Kyiv on the battlefield and in talks.
facts: Ukraine struck a major Russian oil terminal on Sunday, Oct. 18.
Trump said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
Zelensky offered to halt refinery strikes in exchange for Patriot missiles.
Putin proposed a meeting with Trump and Xi next month (Bloomberg).
Four Republican senators and Democrats asked the Pentagon IG to look into Starshield limits.
stories.flag: Who ordered the Starshield speed limits is unresolved; Trump and Rubio deny involvement.
stories.left: Critics argue that the administration is rewarding aggression by waiving Russia sanctions, limiting Ukraine's strikes and leaving it without air defense. They say Trump's attacks on Zelensky echo Moscow's line and that threatening to cut intelligence is coercion of an ally. The Starshield restrictions, they say, need a full investigation. A peace imposed on Kyiv would not hold.
stories.right: Supporters of the administration argue that Ukraine's refinery strikes raise world diesel prices and that Washington has a right to set limits on its own aid. They say Trump is trying to end a war that Europe cannot finance alone and that a summit with Putin is worth testing. Hawkish conservatives, including some Republican senators, disagree and want pressure on Moscow, not on Kyiv. Both camps, in this view, agree the war cannot go on without an endgame.
stories.next: Watch the Pentagon IG request on Starshield and any announcement of a Trump-Putin-Xi meeting next month.

stories.title: Traders expect the Fed to hold on Oct. 28 after a hot September inflation report
stories.summary: September CPI hit 3.7%, but hike odds for next week's meeting have faded as the 10-year yield sits near 5.1%.
story: The Fed meets Oct. 27-28, and traders now see a hold as the likely outcome. CNBC reported Monday that the CME FedWatch tool puts the odds of unchanged rates above 80%, with the 10-year Treasury yield near 5.1%. Live data show the 10-year at 5.14%. After the September CPI report, hike odds had jumped to 41.5% (CNBC), then retreated.

September consumer prices rose 0.6% on the month and 3.7% from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August (Fox Business, NBC News). Energy prices rose 5.2% on the month and 20.4% on the year, and gasoline rose 9.1% on the month. Core CPI was 2.6% on the year, hotter than economists expected. The Fed raised its benchmark rate a quarter point to 3.75%-4% on Sept. 16, its first hike since 2023, and officials penciled in another by year's end (CNN, Fox Business).

Chair Kevin Warsh declined on Oct. 15 to say what he will do. CNN's analysis argued the Fed was "bullied" into hiking by rising yields and inflation. Oxford Economics' Michael Pearce said the Fed "cannot control energy prices." A Washington Examiner op-ed called the September hike badly timed.
The bond market matters for stocks. The 10-year recently reached 5.36% intraday, its highest since 2002 (CNBC), and high yields are part of why chips and AI debt sold off last week.
facts: The Fed meets Oct. 27-28; hold odds are above 80% (CNBC).
September CPI rose 3.7% from a year ago and 0.6% on the month.
Energy prices were up 20.4% on the year; gasoline up 34.2% (Fox Business).
The Fed funds range is 3.75%-4% after the Sept. 16 hike.
The 10-year Treasury yield is 5.14% per live data.
stories.left: Economists on the left argue the inflation is an energy shock from the Iran war, which interest rates cannot fix, and that more hikes risk a recession and job losses without lowering gas prices. They say the burden falls on working families with variable-rate debt. Ending the war and reopening Hormuz would do more than any Fed move. The Fed should look through a supply shock.
stories.right: Conservative economists argue that inflation was already 3.4% in August, before September's energy jump, and that the Fed has to defend its credibility even when energy is the trigger. A Washington Examiner op-ed said the September hike came at the worst possible moment, which shows the Fed's bind. Expanding domestic energy supply would ease the burden, in this view, and the Fed should not rely on the war ending.
stories.next: Watch the Fed's Oct. 28 decision; officials have penciled in another hike by year's end.

stories.title: Chip stocks snap an eight-day losing streak, but credit investors stay nervous about AI debt
stories.summary: The S&P 500 gained 0.41% and the Nasdaq 1.11% on Monday, while CoreWeave and Oracle bonds still price stress.
story: Stocks rebounded Monday after last week's AI-driven selloff. The S&P 500 rose 0.41% to 7,690.73, the Nasdaq gained 1.11% to 26,430.89, and the Dow slipped 0.07% to 51,966.03 (CNBC). Bloomberg reported that the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 1.6%, ending an eight-day losing streak that was its longest in 18 years; CNBC counted nine days. Nvidia gained 1.38% to $217.09.

Credit markets were less relieved. CNBC reported that CoreWeave closed slightly lower despite a Goldman Sachs upgrade to buy with a $106 price target, as its 9.625% bond due 2032 yielded about 14.9%. Oracle holds a BBB- rating from S&P, the lowest investment-grade level, and CNBC puts its five-year credit default swap spread between about 295 and 315 basis points, depending on the report, near high-yield levels. Bloomberg reported that investors are pushing back on Nvidia-backed Nscale's roughly $30 billion IPO target and suggesting $16 billion to $19 billion.

Analysts split on the bounce. CNBC reported that Jim Cramer urged investors not to chase it and to invest only a quarter of the money they want to deploy. BTIG advised using any rebound to cut exposure, while another analyst called the drawdown a buying opportunity (CNBC). CNBC also noted that earnings this week from Tesla and Meta will help decide whether the rebound is real.
Rates matter too. The 10-year yield is 5.14%, and WTI crude is $98.15, both of which weigh on growth stocks.
facts: The semiconductor index rose 1.6%, ending an eight-day streak (Bloomberg).
CoreWeave's 2032 bond yields about 14.9% (CNBC).
Oracle is rated BBB-, one notch above junk at S&P.
Nscale's IPO faces pushback on a $30 billion valuation (Bloomberg).
stories.why: The question is whether AI spending can be financed. Equity buyers returned Monday, but bond investors still demand near-junk yields from the biggest borrowers. For a Nasdaq-heavy portfolio, credit spreads at CoreWeave and Oracle are the early warning to watch, along with the Oct. 28 Fed decision.
stories.next: Watch Tesla (Wednesday), Alphabet and Microsoft (Oct. 28) and Amazon (Oct. 29) earnings, plus Oracle's CDS spread.

stories.title: Amazon jumps about 5% on a Morgan Stanley call, and Tesla rises ahead of Wednesday's earnings
stories.summary: Morgan Stanley named Amazon a top pick with a $350 target; Tesla's results arrive Wednesday after the close.
story: Amazon shares rose 4.98% to $262.45 on Monday after Morgan Stanley named the stock a top pick and raised its price target to $350 from $335 (CNBC). The target implies about 40% upside from Friday's close. Analyst Brian Nowak wrote that AWS's growth and profit runway is under-appreciated, and he pointed to the Bedrock AI platform and robotics-driven efficiencies. LSEG data show 62 of 64 analysts covering Amazon rate it a buy.

Tesla rose 3.76% to $368.06. I found no single news item that explains the move. The company reports on Wednesday, Oct. 21, after the close, and CNBC's preview says the call follows at 5:30 p.m. Analysts expect profit per share to fall 14.5% and revenue to dip about 1% from a year ago. Wolfe Research expects earnings below consensus but is watching a possible SpaceX merger and the robotaxi business as positives (CNBC).
Tesla's deliveries fell 2% from a year ago but beat estimates, which sent the stock higher at the time (CNBC). Amazon reports on Oct. 29.
Both stocks are in the watchlist you set, and each moved more than 3% on a day when the Nasdaq rose 1.1%.
facts: Amazon closed at $262.45, up 4.98% (live data).
Morgan Stanley raised its Amazon target to $350 from $335.
Tesla closed at $368.06, up 3.76%.
Tesla reports Oct. 21 after the close; Amazon on Oct. 29.
Analysts expect Tesla's profit per share to fall 14.5% (CNBC).
stories.flag: No source explained Tesla's Monday gain.
stories.why: Amazon's move shows how much of the AI trade is now a cloud-profit story rather than a chip story. Tesla's quarter will test whether robotaxi and SpaceX talk can offset weaker earnings, which matters if you hold either.
stories.next: Tesla reports Wednesday, Oct. 21, after the close; Amazon follows on Thursday, Oct. 29.

stories.title: NASA says Orion's heat shield performed as expected on Artemis II
stories.summary: Follow-up analysis confirmed early data that the redesigned reentry path cut the char loss seen on Artemis I.
story: NASA said on Oct. 15 that further engineering analysis confirmed the Orion heat shield performed as expected on Artemis II. The capsule reentered at about 39 times the speed of sound, with external temperatures above 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit, while the cabin stayed in the mid-70s (NASA). Artemis II splashed down on April 10, 2026. Space.com quotes commander Reid Wiseman saying the shield survived its trial by fire in good shape.

The concern came from Artemis I, when the shield lost chunks of char. NASA's investigation found the low-permeability Avcoat material built up internal gas pressure during a skip entry, and the gas could not escape, which cracked the material (NASA). For Artemis II, NASA flew a modified trajectory without the skip entry and shortened the downrange distance to limit heating.

Post-flight diver imagery and inspections found char loss significantly reduced in quantity and size, consistent with arc jet ground tests run after Artemis I (NASA). The shield is going to Marshall Space Flight Center for sample extraction and internal X-ray scans.
The result supports using the same shield design and flight path for later missions while the X-ray data come in.
facts: Artemis II splashed down April 10, 2026.
Orion hit about 39 times the speed of sound and above 4,000°F externally.
The cabin stayed in the mid-70s °F.
Artemis I's char loss traced to gas pressure in low-permeability Avcoat during skip entry.
Artemis II used a trajectory with no skip entry.
stories.why: Heat shields cannot be tested at full scale for a lunar return, so flight data is the real proof. A cleaner result supports Artemis III planning, but the internal X-ray scans can still change the picture.
stories.next: Watch for the Marshall X-ray and sample results and any NASA schedule update for the next Artemis mission.

stories.title: Spain extends two nuclear plants because its grid lacks batteries
stories.summary: Spain pushed back the Almaraz shutdown to 2030 while battery capacity rises from 28 MW to 193 MW.
story: On Aug. 14, Spain's government decreed a three-year extension for the two Almaraz reactors, about 2 GW combined. They were scheduled to close in 2027 and 2028 and will now run until 2030 (IEEE Spectrum). The decree blames the crisis in the Middle East. An economist quoted by IEEE Spectrum says the real issue is a grid with booming solar and too little storage.

The numbers back that up. Spain had 28 MW of battery storage at the time of the April 2025 blackout, and 193 MW by April 2026 (IEEE Spectrum). The government is funding 2.2 GW of near-term large-scale storage and has a national target of 22.5 GW, including pumped hydro and other non-battery systems, by 2030. A Bloomberg piece in September said Spain is reaching the limits of clean energy without batteries.

The extension reverses Spain's earlier position. In mid-2025, Bloomberg reported Spain was committed to a 2035 nuclear exit. The nuclear phaseout was a plank of the governing coalition, so the delay has caused conflict inside it (IEEE Spectrum).

The case shows why storage and transmission, not only generation, set the pace of a renewables buildout. IEEE Spectrum notes several other Spanish plants are due to end operations around 2030, so more delays are possible.
facts: The decree was issued Aug. 14 and extends Almaraz by three years to 2030.
The two reactors total about 2 GW.
Battery storage rose from 28 MW at the April 2025 blackout to 193 MW by April 2026.
Spain funds 2.2 GW of near-term storage and targets 22.5 GW by 2030.
The decree cites the Middle East crisis; analysts point to storage gaps.
stories.why: Spain shows that firm power plants often get extended when batteries and transmission arrive late.
stories.next: Watch whether Spain extends other reactors and how fast storage tenders are awarded.

stories.title: Webb finds the home of the most distant fast radio burst, a star-forming dwarf galaxy
stories.summary: The burst FRB 20240304B comes from a galaxy seen about 3 billion years after the Big Bang, more than doubling the distance record.
story: NASA announced on Oct. 8 that the James Webb Space Telescope located the host galaxy of FRB 20240304B, the most distant fast radio burst found so far. The MeerTRAP team detected the burst on March 4, 2024, with South Africa's MeerKAT radio telescope. Ground telescopes could not see a galaxy at the position, so the team used Webb. The study was published in the journal Science (NASA).

Webb's NIRCam found a small dwarf galaxy actively forming stars and confirmed a redshift of 2.148, placing the burst about 3 billion years after the Big Bang. Space.com reports the galaxy lies around 11 billion light-years away and that the result more than doubles the previous distance record (Space.com).

The earlier record holder, FRB 20220610A, flashed in a collection of galaxies when the universe was about 5 billion years old, and Hubble studied it (NASA). Space.com says scientists were surprised by the source.
Distant bursts also work as probes of the gas between galaxies.
facts: The burst is FRB 20240304B, detected March 4, 2024, by MeerKAT.
Webb measured a redshift of 2.148.
The host is a small dwarf galaxy actively forming stars.
The burst is about 3 billion years after the Big Bang (NASA).
The paper appeared in Science; NASA's release is dated Oct. 8, 2026.
stories.why: Fast radio bursts at this distance let astronomers measure the gas between galaxies and test what kinds of stars produce them. Webb's infrared sensitivity found a galaxy that ground telescopes missed.
stories.next: Watch for other distant bursts from MeerKAT and follow-up from Webb and Hubble.

stories.title: Perseverance passes Opportunity for the longest drive by any rover on another world
stories.summary: NASA's rover logged 28.10 miles on Oct. 11, using autonomous driving for more than 90% of the distance.
story: NASA's Perseverance rover set an off-world driving record on Oct. 11, 2026. Its odometer reached 28.10 miles (45.22 km), passing the 28.06 miles (45.16 km) logged by Opportunity (NASA, Space.com). Opportunity needed about 14 years to cover that ground, and Perseverance has been on Mars for roughly 5.5 years.

The difference is autonomy. Perseverance has driven more than 90% of its distance using AutoNav, which evaluates terrain on board, compared with about 5% for Opportunity and Spirit's first system (NASA). Its longest single autonomous drive is about 1,350.7 feet (411.7 m), recorded June 19, 2025. Curiosity has driven more than 23.65 miles (38.07 km).
NASA approved the rover's first extended mission, running through roughly the end of 2028. Mission engineer Maimone said the team is looking at up to 100 kilometers in total (Space.com).
The rover is still exploring, and NASA says it could keep driving well past this mark.
facts: Perseverance's odometer read 28.10 miles (45.22 km) on Oct. 11.
Opportunity's record was 28.06 miles (45.16 km).
More than 90% of the driving used AutoNav.
The longest single autonomous drive is about 1,350.7 feet.
The extended mission runs through about the end of 2028.
stories.why: Autonomous driving is what lets a rover cover ground without waiting for commands across tens of millions of miles. The same software approach will matter for future lunar and Mars rovers.
stories.next: Watch the rover's next sample targets and the 100 km goal.

stories.title: Anthropic pledges 5% of its shares to a public benefit fund, and Musk answers with a SpaceX giveaway
stories.summary: Anthropic's fund needs stockholder approval; Musk says he will give every US child a SpaceX share next year.
story: Anthropic said on Oct. 18 that it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new Public Benefit Fund, subject to stockholder approval (CNBC, TechCrunch, Bloomberg). The board could add roughly 2 percentage points for every 50% rise in value above an undisclosed baseline. Axios estimates the pledge would be worth $100 billion if Anthropic reaches a $2 trillion valuation at its IPO.

The fund would be a wholly owned limited liability company, not a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It could make large donations to nonprofits or direct distributions to specific groups, and its equity would not be used for lobbying or political giving (Axios, TechCrunch). Anthropic said it will share more on structure and governance in the coming months. CNBC also reported that Anthropic told investors third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion ahead of an IPO reportedly slated for November.

Elon Musk replied on X: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public… This is what I will be doing." On Monday he posted that he will give one SpaceX share to "every kid in America" next year, without saying how (NBC News). CNBC estimates the cost at about $10.5 billion, using SpaceX's $146.03 Friday close and 72 million children. Trump thanked Musk and referred to Trump Accounts (Washington Examiner), which now accept stock donations from charities (NBC News). Anthropic stayed silent on whether it would give shares directly (Fox Business).
Anthropic makes Claude, the assistant that compiles this feed, so weigh my framing accordingly. The story matters because AI companies are now competing to show how the gains from AI will be shared.
facts: Anthropic plans to commit 5% of shares to a Public Benefit Fund, pending stockholder approval.
The fund would be an LLC and would not fund lobbying.
Anthropic told investors Q3 revenue is $16.8 billion (CNBC).
Musk pledged one SpaceX share to every US child next year; details are missing.
CNBC estimates Musk's pledge at about $10.5 billion.
stories.flag: Fund structure, governance and the baseline for added shares were not disclosed; Musk has not said how the giveaway would work.
stories.why: The pledges set a precedent for how AI wealth could be redistributed as job disruption fears grow. For markets, the fund adds an IPO governance detail investors must price, and Cramer named a successful Anthropic IPO as a hurdle for the AI trade.
stories.next: Watch for Anthropic's governance details and IPO timing in November, and for Treasury guidance on Trump Account donations.

stories.title: Nvidia releases open-weight models for enterprise agents and local AI PCs
stories.summary: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL has 120 billion parameters; two Bolt models run locally on RTX Spark PCs and DGX Spark.
story: Nvidia launched new open-weight models on Oct. 19 aimed at enterprise agents and local PCs (TechCrunch). Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120-billion-parameter model for enterprise agents. Nvidia says it matches Nemotron 3 Ultra on instruction following and tool-use accuracy with fewer parameters, and it names Skydance, EY, Ramp, CrowdStrike, Perplexity and Salesforce as users.

Two lightweight Bolt models run locally on AI PCs with the RTX Spark chip and on DGX Spark workstations. Bolt 74B-A9B targets local agentic work such as multistep reasoning, tool calling and web browsing. Bolt E4B targets conversational agents. Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, and Bolt E4B arrives later this month (TechCrunch).

The release continues a strategy CNBC has tracked. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a free model for PCs, came out in August, and in March Nvidia announced NemoClaw, an enterprise agent platform built on the open-source OpenClaw framework. CNBC described Meta and Nvidia in August as planting a "very firm flag" in the open-weight race led by Chinese labs. The benchmark claims here are Nvidia's own and are not independently verified.
Nvidia shares gained 1.38% to $217.09 on Monday. Its next earnings date is Nov. 18.
facts: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL has 120 billion parameters.
Bolt 74B-A9B and Bolt E4B are built for local agents on RTX Spark PCs and DGX Spark.
Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now; Bolt E4B comes later this month.
Named users include Skydance, EY, Ramp, CrowdStrike, Perplexity and Salesforce.
Nvidia reports earnings on Nov. 18.
stories.flag: Benchmark claims come from Nvidia and have not been independently verified.
stories.why: Open models that run on a desktop let companies keep agent data on site and cut cloud costs. They also give Nvidia a way to sell hardware, since the models are tuned for its chips.
stories.next: Watch for independent benchmarks and for Bolt E4B's release later this month.

briefs: Anthropic says small AI models are "months away" from copying themselves across home devices; in one test, a Google Gemma4-26B-A4B model ran across 15 cheap Android TV boxes, and Anthropic says no fully rogue replicator exists yet (CNBC).
Judge Ana Reyes rejected the Justice Department's recusal request as "baseless" and weighed a narrower order on Trump's East Potomac golf course plan; Trump says work starts Nov. 15 (CNN, The Hill).

The CDC counts 4,080 measles cases this year, the most since 1991, and is sending a disease detective and nearly $4 million to Pennsylvania, where a sixth measles-related death was reported (NBC News).
PayPal will cut 251 jobs at its San Jose headquarters, effective Oct. 30, according to a state notice (San Francisco Chronicle).
A tritium betavoltaic battery with 48 cells powered a sensor payload on the BOHR CubeSat, a possible power source for future lunar bases (IEEE Spectrum).
